implementation_notes: Go's first-class channels make the return address a field of the request value: the requester allocates a reply channel per request, the worker sends the answer into it — no header, no broker, no name resolution. This is the shape the EIP catalog itself demonstrates in Go and the natural realization for in-process worker pools and pipelines; if requests must leave the process, switch to the NATS variant or the transport's reply-to property, because a channel cannot be serialized.

variants.idiom_name: request struct carrying a reply chan field
variants.implementation_notes: Go's first-class channels make the return address a field of the request value: the requester allocates a reply channel per request, the worker sends the answer into it — no header, no broker, no name resolution. This is the shape the EIP catalog itself demonstrates in Go and the natural realization for in-process worker pools and pipelines; if requests must leave the process, switch to the NATS variant or the transport's reply-to property, because a channel cannot be serialized.
pitfalls: An unbuffered reply channel pins the worker until the requester receives: size the buffer or one slow caller stalls the pool.
A requester that abandons its channel blocks the worker forever, since send has no timeout — select on a context or use a buffer of one.
A channel cannot cross a process boundary; using this shape as a protocol placeholder is a design bug, not an optimization.

variants.name: NATS reply subject (Msg.Reply) with an auto-subscribed inbox
variants.implementation_notes: NATS carries the return address in the protocol: nc.Request creates a unique inbox subject, subscribes to it and publishes the request with that subject as the reply, while the service answers with nc.Publish(msg.Reply, ...). This is the distributed counterpart of the channel variant and the reason request-reply needs no service-side configuration; use it whenever requests cross hosts, and reserve the channel variant for in-process work.
pitfalls: The inbox is subscribed only for the duration of Request: a slow service loses the reply after the timeout even though it eventually answers.
Newer clients report 'no responders' when nobody subscribes to the subject; without it an unreachable service looks like a hang until the timeout fires.
A reply per request doubles message traffic — for throughput-sensitive paths batch responses or use JetStream with a durable reply channel.
